army.title: The Generals Grow Restless
army.question: Field Marshal, will you shield the army's budget or risk the officers?
army.body: The service commanders met in Nasr City without you. They want the military budget sealed from parliament, no officer before a civilian court, and no more soldiers sent against crowds. Lieutenant General Sami Anan has asked for a full Council session on Thursday.

answers.text: Seal the military budget from any civilian review
answers.sub: The army's economy stays beyond parliament's reach, by decree.

reasons.army: Our factories, land and aid stay ours alone.
reasons.moi: A strong army shields the police beside it.
reasons.mb: An army above parliament makes our majority hollow.
reasons.rev: A state within the state, written into law.
reasons.usa: Congress wants civilian oversight, not a sealed ledger.

answers.gripWhy: Ruling by decree on the budget hardens the Council.

answers.text: Open the budget to an elected parliament
answers.sub: Deputies may read and vote the defence accounts.

reasons.army: Civilian scrutiny of our budget is the red line.
reasons.rev: At last the generals answer to the people.
reasons.usa: Real civilian control, the transition Washington asked for.
reasons.mb: Parliament's power grows, and we will lead parliament.
reasons.fel: Open ledgers today mean open ledgers for tycoons tomorrow.

answers.gripWhy: Oversight of the army loosens the Council's hold.

answers.text: Trade army autonomy for the Brotherhood's election calendar
answers.sub: A quiet pact: the Brothers vote, the barracks stay sealed.

reasons.army: A partner who leaves our budget alone will do.
reasons.mb: Elections on time is all the Guidance Bureau needs.
reasons.salc: A Brotherhood deal leaves the Nour Party outside.
reasons.rev: The generals and the Brothers divide the revolution.
reasons.ksa: Riyadh did not pay to seat the Brotherhood.

mb.title: The Brotherhood Wants Dates
mb.question: Will you fix the election date, or face the Brotherhood in Tahrir?
mb.body: Brotherhood offices in every governorate have hired buses. Mohamed Badie's statement demands a fixed election calendar, an end to talk of supra-constitutional charters, and the right of the largest bloc to form a government. The Friday of 'Handing over power' is called for this week.

answers.text: Publish a fixed calendar and drop the charter
answers.sub: Votes on set dates; no binding principles over parliament.

reasons.mb: The ballot box, on our timetable, decides everything.
reasons.salc: Early votes favour the Islamist parties, us included.
reasons.army: Without a charter, an elected majority can touch us.
reasons.fel: Quick elections hand the provinces to the Brotherhood.
reasons.ksa: A fast road to a Brotherhood parliament alarms Riyadh.

answers.text: Ban the march and arrest the organisers
answers.sub: Military Police at the squares; Guidance Bureau men detained.

reasons.mb: The prisons of 1954 and 1965 open again.
reasons.moi: The men we hunted for decades, back where they belong.
reasons.army: The street learns who still commands it.
reasons.ksa: Exactly the firmness Riyadh expects from Cairo.
reasons.qat: Doha's allies jailed; Al Jazeera will show it all.
reasons.usa: Arrests of a party contesting elections worry Washington.

answers.gripWhy: Mass arrests and a march banned by order.

answers.text: Call a national dialogue of all parties
answers.sub: Liberals, Copts and youth seated beside the Brotherhood.

reasons.mb: Talk is a delay dressed as consensus.
reasons.salc: Seated with secularists as one voice among many.
reasons.rev: At least the youth get a seat this time.
reasons.usa: Inclusive dialogue is what Washington has been urging.
reasons.fel: Dialogue slows the Brotherhood and leaves room for us.

answers.gripWhy: Opening the table to every party eases tension.

salc.title: Hands Off Article 2
salc.question: Will you swear Article 2 stays untouched, or let secularists rewrite it?
salc.body: Preachers on al-Nas and al-Rahma call the Council's constitutional plans an assault on Islam. Yasser Borhami wants a written pledge that Article 2 and the principles of Sharia are beyond amendment. Buses from Alexandria and the Delta are booked for Friday.

answers.text: Pledge in writing that Article 2 is untouchable
answers.sub: Sharia's principles stay the source of law, sealed by you.

reasons.salc: The law of God is placed beyond the secularists.
reasons.mb: The Islamic reference is secured without our fighting.
reasons.rev: The Council bows to preachers, not to citizens.
reasons.usa: Washington hears the Copts' alarm in every cable.
reasons.fel: The preachers set terms; the old business class worries.

answers.text: Insist the new constitution guarantees equal citizenship
answers.sub: Muslims and Copts equal before law; Article 2 left open.

reasons.salc: Tampering with Article 2 is the red line.
reasons.rev: Crescent and cross, equal citizens, as in Tahrir.
reasons.usa: Equal rights for Copts reassures Congress.
reasons.mb: An open Article 2 hands secularists a weapon.
reasons.ksa: Riyadh will not see Cairo drift from Sharia.

answers.gripWhy: A citizenship pledge opens the constitutional debate.

answers.text: Let al-Azhar's scholars arbitrate the religion clauses
answers.sub: Ahmed el-Tayeb's institution, not street preachers, frames Article 2.

reasons.salc: Al-Azhar's state sheikhs never spoke for the Salaf.
reasons.mb: An Islamic reference with no Salafist veto suits us.
reasons.army: A state institution keeps religion in orderly hands.
reasons.rev: Clerics, of any rank, should not write citizenship.
reasons.qat: A moderate Islamic framing is what Doha backs.

moi.title: The Police Stay Home
moi.question: Will you shield police officers from trial, or let prosecutors in?
moi.body: Half the police stations in Cairo stand empty. Officers say they will not patrol while colleagues face murder charges for January. Their club demands the prosecutions stopped, State Security files kept sealed and the army standing behind them.

answers.text: Halt the prosecutions of officers for January
answers.sub: Cases frozen; the ranks return to the streets.

reasons.moi: Our men are shielded; we go back to work.
reasons.army: Police on patrol means soldiers back in barracks.
reasons.fel: Order returns, and old friends stay out of court.
reasons.rev: The killers of our martyrs walk free.
reasons.usa: Impunity for killing protesters is Washington's red line.

answers.gripWhy: Impunity for police restores the old fear on the streets.

answers.text: Purge the senior ranks and restructure the ministry
answers.sub: Generals retired, State Security files opened to prosecutors.

reasons.moi: A purge of officers is the red line.
reasons.army: Purges spread; the army fears its own turn.
reasons.rev: The police state dismantled, as January demanded.
reasons.usa: Security sector reform is the transition Washington funds.
reasons.mb: Our old jailers lose their files and their posts.

answers.gripWhy: Breaking the security apparatus loosens control of the street.

answers.text: Raise constables' pay, but let the trials run
answers.sub: Junior police bought back; commanders still face the court.

reasons.moi: The ranks are paid, though the generals still worry.
reasons.rev: Trials go on; pay is not impunity.
reasons.army: The treasury favours police over the barracks.
reasons.fel: Old allies in the ministry still face the cage.

fel.title: The Remnants Close Ranks
fel.question: Will you block the isolation law, or let the old party's men be barred?
fel.body: Former NDP deputies have stopped paying workers in Sohag and Qena. Tycoons are moving dollars to Dubai. Their price is plain: no political isolation law, no new corruption cases, and their families free to stand in the elections.

answers.text: Shelve the isolation law and new corruption cases
answers.sub: Old notables may stand; their fortunes stay untouched.

reasons.fel: Our families, money and votes stay in play.
reasons.army: The provincial notables are the army's natural allies.
reasons.ksa: Riyadh trusts the men of the old order.
reasons.rev: The remnants of the regime are pardoned in all but name.
reasons.mb: The old party's machine is set loose against us.

answers.text: Pass the isolation law against NDP leaders
answers.sub: Ten years barred from office for the old leadership.

reasons.fel: Barring NDP members from office is the red line.
reasons.moi: Old patrons of the ministry pushed out of power.
reasons.rev: The men of the old regime cannot return.
reasons.mb: Our strongest provincial rivals leave the ballot.
reasons.usa: A clean break satisfies the democracy lobby, mostly.

answers.text: Confiscate looted land and return it to the state
answers.sub: Tycoons' desert plots and privatised factories seized for the public.

reasons.fel: Confiscation of land and contracts is ruin.
reasons.rev: The stolen wealth goes back to the people.
reasons.army: Seizures set a precedent for the army's own firms.
reasons.ksa: Gulf investors in those plots lose their money.
reasons.usa: Nationalisation scares every foreign investor away.

rev.title: Down With Military Rule
rev.question: Will you end military trials for civilians, or clear the square?
rev.body: Tents are back in Tahrir. The Revolution Youth Coalition and April 6 demand an end to referring civilians to military courts, the Emergency Law lifted and a date for the army to leave power. Marches are called for Alexandria and Suez.

answers.text: End military trials and lift the Emergency Law
answers.sub: Civilians back before civilian judges; detainees' cases reviewed.

reasons.rev: The revolution's first demand, finally met.
reasons.usa: Ending emergency rule is the step Congress demanded.
reasons.qat: Freedom in Cairo, broadcast proudly on Al Jazeera.
reasons.moi: Without emergency powers our arrests mean nothing.
reasons.army: Military prosecutors were our fastest tool of order.

answers.gripWhy: Emergency powers and military courts are given up.

answers.text: Clear the square with the Military Police
answers.sub: Tents torn down at dawn; organisers before military prosecutors.

reasons.rev: Down with military rule, louder in every city.
reasons.moi: The square cleared, and the state feared again.
reasons.ksa: Order in Cairo is order in the Gulf.
reasons.army: Soldiers dragged into policing the street once more.
reasons.usa: Pictures of soldiers clearing tents reach Congress.
reasons.qat: Al Jazeera's cameras will show every tent torn down.

answers.gripWhy: The square is cleared by force at dawn.

answers.text: Grant a minimum wage and receive the youth
answers.sub: A 700-pound floor for public workers; coalition leaders received.

reasons.rev: Bread and social justice, with a seat at the table.
reasons.usa: Dialogue with the youth looks like a real transition.
reasons.fel: Wage floors fall on the employers' payrolls.
reasons.mb: The youth are courted while we are kept waiting.

usa.title: Washington Conditions the Aid
usa.question: Will you meet Washington's terms, or risk the $1.3 billion?
usa.body: The embassy's political officer brings a message from the Secretary of State. Congress wants proof of a real transition before releasing $1.3 billion in military aid: a fixed handover date, American NGOs left alone and no more protesters killed. Without it, no waiver.

answers.text: Fix the handover date and free the NGOs
answers.sub: A public calendar; NGO cases dropped; American staff may leave.

reasons.usa: A credible transition and our citizens safe.
reasons.rev: A date for the generals to go, in writing.
reasons.army: Washington dictates the calendar of our withdrawal.
reasons.moi: Foreign-funded agitators walk free on our files.
reasons.ksa: Cairo bending to Washington's democracy agenda irritates Riyadh.

answers.gripWhy: A public handover date loosens the Council's hold.

answers.text: Refuse dictation and denounce foreign funding
answers.sub: State television attacks American meddling; NGO cases proceed.

reasons.usa: Prosecuting Americans is Washington's red line.
reasons.army: Sovereignty before aid; the army bows to no one.
reasons.moi: Our case against the foreign NGOs goes ahead.
reasons.ksa: Cairo standing up to Washington pleases Riyadh.
reasons.rev: Every activist is now branded a foreign agent.

answers.gripWhy: A campaign against foreign funding tightens control.

answers.text: Cancel American programmes and go it alone
answers.sub: No IMF, no USAID; Egypt pays its own way.

reasons.usa: Cairo walks away from thirty years of partnership.
reasons.army: Without American spare parts the tanks stand still.
reasons.fel: Tycoons lose the American contracts they lived on.
reasons.rev: Independence from Washington, as Nasser would have it.
reasons.salc: No American hand in Egypt's affairs.

ksa.title: Riyadh Holds Its Deposits
ksa.question: Will you spare Mubarak and curb the Brotherhood to keep Riyadh's money?
ksa.body: Riyadh's promised deposits sit unpaid at the Central Bank. The King is angered by demands to put Mubarak on trial and by Brotherhood leaders courting Doha. The counsellor says the money moves when Mubarak is spared and the Brotherhood checked.

answers.text: Spare Mubarak a public trial; keep him in Sharm
answers.sub: Medical seclusion in Sharm el-Sheikh; no cage, no cameras.

reasons.ksa: An old friend spared humiliation; the deposits move.
reasons.fel: The old president spared means the old order spared.
reasons.rev: The tyrant escapes justice; Tahrir will rise again.
reasons.mb: The Council protects Mubarak and bows to Riyadh.
reasons.usa: Shielding Mubarak looks like restoration to Congress.

answers.gripWhy: Overriding the trial demand by decree.

answers.text: Favour the Nour Party over the Brotherhood
answers.sub: Salafist preachers get airtime and licences; Brotherhood squeezed.

reasons.ksa: Our Salafist friends check Doha's Brotherhood.
reasons.salc: Finally the state treats us as the Brotherhood's equal.
reasons.mb: The Council splits the Islamist camp against us.
reasons.rev: Preachers promoted while the youth are ignored.
reasons.qat: Riyadh's clients pushed ahead of Doha's allies.

answers.text: Let the courts try Mubarak like any citizen
answers.sub: Justice runs its course; Riyadh's deposits wait.

reasons.ksa: Mubarak in the dock is an insult to the King.
reasons.fel: If Mubarak falls in court, so do his men.
reasons.rev: No one above the law, not even Mubarak.
reasons.usa: Due process for the old regime reads well in Congress.
reasons.mb: Our old persecutor faces judgment at last.

qat.title: Al Jazeera's Cameras Turn
qat.question: Will you open the door to Doha, or shut Al Jazeera's office?
qat.body: Al Jazeera Mubasher Misr runs every clash live, with Brotherhood guests on the hour. Doha's envoy offers investment and deposits if elections go ahead on time and the Brotherhood is left free. The Interior Ministry wants the Cairo bureau closed.

answers.text: Welcome Doha's money and keep the vote on time
answers.sub: Qatari deposits arrive; Brotherhood freedoms guaranteed.

reasons.qat: Doha's influence in Cairo grows with its money.
reasons.mb: Our Gulf friend pays, and the vote stays on schedule.
reasons.ksa: A Qatari foothold in Cairo is Riyadh's nightmare.
reasons.moi: The Brotherhood made untouchable by foreign money.
reasons.army: Doha buys a say in Egypt's politics.

answers.text: Raid the Cairo bureau and seize its equipment
answers.sub: Broadcast licences pulled; the channel goes dark in Egypt.

reasons.qat: A crackdown on our channel is a crackdown on us.
reasons.mb: Our loudest platform is silenced.
reasons.moi: No more live footage of every clash.
reasons.ksa: Al Jazeera stirred the Arab street; good riddance.
reasons.usa: Raiding journalists embarrasses Washington's partner.
reasons.rev: The cameras that protected Tahrir are gone.

answers.gripWhy: A broadcaster raided and silenced by order.

answers.text: Let every channel broadcast, but decline Doha's money
answers.sub: A free press, with no foreign deposits buying influence.

reasons.qat: Doha's offer refused in front of the Arab world.
reasons.mb: Our patron's money turned away at the door.
reasons.rev: Free screens, no Gulf strings attached.
reasons.usa: Press freedom without Gulf patronage reassures Washington.
reasons.ksa: Doha shut out of Cairo's treasury pleases Riyadh.

answers.gripWhy: Every channel left free to broadcast.

elections.title: The People's Assembly Vote
elections.question: Field Marshal, will you open the polls on schedule?
elections.body: Ballot boxes and judges are ready for three rounds across 27 governorates. The Freedom and Justice lists draw the biggest rallies. The Salafist Nour Party is close behind. 498 elected seats are at stake.

answers.text: Hold the elections on schedule under judges
answers.sub: Three rounds, judicial supervision, foreign observers admitted.

reasons.mb: Our organisation will fill the new parliament.
reasons.salc: The Nour Party enters parliament in force.
reasons.usa: A real vote is the transition Washington wanted.
reasons.fel: Without the old machine, our clans face the Islamists.
reasons.moi: Policing three rounds while the Brotherhood takes over.

answers.gripWhy: Free, supervised elections open the field.

answers.text: Postpone the vote until order returns
answers.sub: Mandate extended by declaration; streets first, ballots later.

reasons.mb: Cancelling the vote is the red line.
reasons.salc: Our first chance at parliament snatched away.
reasons.rev: The generals never meant to leave.
reasons.army: More time to secure the army's place first.
reasons.ksa: No Brotherhood parliament; Riyadh is relieved.

answers.gripWhy: Elections delayed by military decree.

answers.text: Draw districts for the notables and clans
answers.sub: Large rural constituencies; old NDP families win individual seats.

reasons.army: A parliament of notables will not touch the barracks.
reasons.mb: The map is drawn to cheat us of seats.

reasons.usa: Observers will call the map rigged.

answers.gripWhy: A rigged map keeps the old order in charge.

elections.question: Will you hold the Shura vote, or spare the country another ballot?
elections.body: The upper house is due to be elected in two stages. Turnout fears are high after weeks of People's Assembly rounds. The Brotherhood wants it done before the constituent assembly is chosen; the generals want time.

answers.sub: Both houses complete; parliament may choose the constituent assembly.

reasons.salc: More seats for the Nour Party, more say on Sharia.

reasons.fel: Another round the old notables cannot win.

answers.gripWhy: Another free vote widens elected power.

reasons.army: We shape the constitution before the Islamists can.
reasons.ksa: The Brotherhood's march slowed is Riyadh's wish.
reasons.mb: Cancelling a vote is the red line.
reasons.salc: Our seats in the upper house are taken away.
reasons.rev: Another delay, another sign the generals stay.

reasons.usa: The promised handover to an elected civilian, on time.
reasons.rev: A civilian president, whatever the flaws of the race.
reasons.army: An elected president may claim the army's command.
reasons.ksa: A Brotherhood president is a real risk now.

answers.gripWhy: The presidency opened to a free vote.

answers.sub: Handover postponed; the generals rule another six months.

reasons.moi: The Council stays, and so does our cover.
reasons.mb: Cancelling the vote is the red line.
reasons.rev: Down with military rule, now in every square.
reasons.usa: A broken handover pledge puts the aid at risk.

answers.gripWhy: Military rule extended by decree.

answers.text: Lean on the commission to favour Shafik
answers.sub: State media, governors and counting rooms back the general.

reasons.fel: Our man in the palace, our fortunes safe.
reasons.army: A former air force commander as president suits us.
reasons.mb: A stolen presidency means the street.

reasons.qat: Al Jazeera will call it a counter-revolution.

answers.gripWhy: The count bent by the state apparatus.

history.title: The First Declaration

history.question: Field Marshal, how will you hold the state until elections?

answers.sub: Parliament dissolved, amendments drafted, the Council holds all power.

reasons.army: Power stays with the high command, on its own timetable.
reasons.moi: A strong hand above means police can return.
reasons.mb: The rigged parliament is gone and elections are promised.

history.title: The Cage

reasons.rev: The channel that showed Tahrir stays on air.
reasons.ksa: A Doha foothold in Cairo is Riyadh's nightmare.

situations.title: The Fund's Conditions
situations.question: Will you sign the IMF's $3 billion loan and its conditions?
situations.body: The IMF offers a $3 billion stand-by loan, now in negotiation, with Washington's blessing. Reserves have lost $5 billion since February. The conditions touch fuel subsidies and the state firms. The generals bristle; the business elite wants it signed this month.

reasons.army: IMF auditors will ask about state and military firms.

reasons.salc: Interest-bearing debt is usury, forbidden in Islam.

situations.title: Seats or Lists

carrier.name: Major Khaled Ezzat
carrier.role: legal aide in the Council's constitutional office

situations.question: Individual seats or party lists: which law will you sign?
situations.body: Mamdouh Shahin's draft election law sits on your desk. Individual seats favour the old ruling party's provincial families, with their clans and cash. Party lists favour the Brotherhood's discipline. The youth coalition, still forming parties, begs for more time before any vote.

answers.text: Keep individual seats, as under the old republic

reasons.fel: Clans and cash win individual seats; the remnants return.
reasons.army: Familiar notables make a parliament the army can manage.
reasons.moi: Provincial police know these families well.
reasons.mb: Individual seats blunt the Brotherhood's party machine.
reasons.rev: The NDP's families walk back into parliament.
reasons.salc: New Salafist parties cannot win clan seats.

answers.gripWhy: The old electoral machine survives intact.

reasons.army: More months for the Council to shape the transition.
reasons.mb: Delay is the old trick; the Brotherhood wants the vote now.

situations.title: Fire at the Shrines

carrier.name: Sheikh Abdel Rahman Shawky
carrier.role: deputy of a Sufi order in Tanta

situations.question: The shrines burn. Will you guard them, or leave the preachers alone?
situations.body: Zealots have smashed Sufi tombs in Qalyubia and set fire to a shrine in Alexandria. Grand Imam Ahmed el-Tayeb asks the state to guard every shrine. The Salafist Call disowns the attacks but defends its preaching against grave veneration. Police officers ask for orders.

reasons.moi: The street belongs to sheikhs, not officers.
reasons.army: Order handed to preachers looks like a state in retreat.

reasons.salc: A code of conduct fences in Salafist preaching.

reasons.rev: Clerics negotiate while shrines burn.

reasons.moi: Its officers return to guard posts with full authority.
reasons.army: Order restored without soldiers on the street.

reasons.ksa: Riyadh dislikes Salafist preachers in Egyptian jails.

answers.gripWhy: State Security reopens its files on preachers.

situations.title: Al-Azhar's Document
situations.question: Will you make al-Azhar's Document the shared basis of the constitution?
situations.body: Al-Azhar's Document on the Future of Egypt endorses a modern, democratic, constitutional state with Sharia principles as the main source of legislation. The Brotherhood endorses it. answers.sub: Sharia principles and a democratic state, as al-Azhar wrote.

reasons.usa: A democratic, constitutional state reassures Washington.
reasons.qat: Doha's allies win a shared charter.
reasons.salc: Its 'modern state' smuggles secularism past Article 2.
reasons.rev: A cleric's charter decides what the people should write.

answers.text: Amend it: the rulings of Sharia, not merely principles

answers.gripWhy: The state, not parliament, sets the founding charter.

situations.title: Staging Mubarak's Trial
situations.question: Field Marshal, where will you put your old commander on trial?
situations.body: Hosni Mubarak lies detained in a Sharm el-Sheikh hospital. The indictment names him with Habib el-Adly and six police commanders. Riyadh's envoys ask for dignity. The martyrs' families camp in Tahrir and want the cage at the Police Academy, on live television.

reasons.fel: Our patron spared the cage; our own trials may soften.

reasons.mb: Closed doors let the old regime bargain for its own.
reasons.usa: Hidden proceedings look like impunity to Congress.

answers.gripWhy: Courts closed to press and public.

answers.text: Cage him at the Police Academy, cameras live.
answers.sub: Open trial in Cairo; Maspero broadcasts every session.

reasons.usa: Open justice on camera answers critics in Congress.

reasons.moi: Six of our commanders shown to the nation as killers.
reasons.army: The cage reminds officers who might stand in it next.

answers.gripWhy: Justice opened to the public eye.

answers.sub: The Mubarak family's assets frozen and claimed for the treasury.

reasons.rev: Trial and restitution: the stolen billions come home.
reasons.mb: The plundered wealth of Egypt returns to its people.
reasons.fel: If his fortune falls, every tycoon's fortune is next.
reasons.ksa: Stripping a former president shames every Gulf friend.
reasons.army: Asset seizures invite questions about the military economy.

situations.title: The Friday of Kandahar
situations.question: Field Marshal, will you thank the sheikhs or curb their slogans?
situations.body: On 29 July Tahrir filled with Salafist banners, Saudi flags and the chant 'Islamiya, Islamiya'. Liberal parties walked out and call it the 'Friday of Kandahar'. The Salafist Call says its marshals kept perfect order. Riyadh's embassy counts its friends.

answers.sub: Maspero thanks the sheikhs; their banners stay in the square.

reasons.rev: The Council courts the beards to drown out Tahrir.
reasons.mb: Praise for the Salafists splits the Islamist vote from us.

reasons.fel: Pulpit power in the provinces threatens our clans' votes.

answers.sub: A civil-state rule for squares and campaigns, enforced by police.

reasons.usa: Rules for a pluralist campaign reassure the State Department.
reasons.moi: Clear rules give our officers grounds to clear squares.

reasons.ksa: Our flag treated as contraband by the Council we fund.

situations.title: Blood on the Eilat Border
situations.question: Field Marshal, five border policemen are dead. How will you answer Israel?

reasons.qat: Al Jazeera's heroes: Cairo stands up to Israel.

reasons.army: Treaty policy handed to parties invades the army's domain.
reasons.ksa: A Brotherhood parliament steering foreign policy worries Riyadh.

situations.title: Summoned for a Post

carrier.role: Organiser, No to Military Trials campaign

situations.title: The Nation on Strike

situations.title: Flowers for Faces

carrier.name: Hany Ragab
carrier.role: clerk at the High Elections Commission

situations.question: Field Marshal, will you let the pulpits campaign, or ban religious slogans?
situations.body: Nour Party posters in Alexandria show a rose where its women candidates' faces should be. Friday sermons in Kafr el-Sheikh name the party list. The Wafd and the Egyptian Bloc petition for a ban on religious slogans. Freedom and Justice organisers say Salafists are taking their mosques.

answers.text: Let the preachers speak; faith is no crime
answers.sub: The pulpit stays open; no commission ruling on slogans.

reasons.salc: Our sheikhs reach voters the Brotherhood never could.
reasons.mb: Salafist sermons strip our mosques of our own voters.
reasons.rev: Mosques turned into campaign offices; the revolution drowns.
reasons.usa: Washington wants a vote that looks like a civil contest.
reasons.ksa: Preachers Riyadh admires win a free hearing.

answers.text: Enforce the ban on religious slogans in campaigns
answers.sub: Commission fines posters and sermons; mosques stay out of the race.

reasons.usa: A civil campaign is the transition promised to Congress.

reasons.fel: Old-party candidates gain when the sheikhs fall quiet.

reasons.salc: A rule cut to the Brotherhood's measure, against us.
reasons.rev: Religion still rules the campaign, only more politely.
reasons.qat: Doha's friends in Freedom and Justice keep their edge.
reasons.ksa: The Brotherhood favoured over Riyadh's Salafist friends.

situations.title: The Woman in the Street

carrier.name: Major Ayman Salah
carrier.role: aide in the military spokesman's office

situations.question: The footage is everywhere, Field Marshal. Will you apologise or blame infiltrators?
situations.body: Military police cleared the cabinet sit-in on Qasr al-Aini Street. Al Jazeera shows soldiers beating protesters and dragging a veiled woman across the asphalt. Hillary Clinton condemns it before the world. Thousands of women march to Tahrir. State television blames paid infiltrators.

answers.text: Apologise to Egypt's women; refer the soldiers for investigation
answers.sub: A Council apology on air; soldiers handed to investigators.

reasons.army: Soldiers offered up to the cameras humiliates the uniform.

situations.title: The Advisory Council
situations.question: The Brotherhood has walked out. Will you let the advisers shape the assembly?
situations.body: You created a 30-member Advisory Council of public figures to propose how the constituent assembly is chosen. Freedom and Justice withdrew its delegate within days, saying only elected deputies may choose. Liberal and old-party advisers want quotas binding the Islamist majority.

reasons.salc: Our 123 seats get their share of the pen.

reasons.army: A charter written without us may reach our budget.
reasons.qat: Doha's allies win the pen of the constitution.

answers.text: Let the advisers set quotas for women, Copts, professions

reasons.rev: A constitution for all Egyptians, not one bloc.
reasons.usa: Inclusive drafting is what Washington asked for.
reasons.mb: Unelected men binding the people's deputies is our red line.
reasons.salc: Quotas for churches and secularists dilute Article 2's guardians.
reasons.fel: Our men sit among the advisers and the professions.

reasons.moi: A strong Council means a protected ministry.

situations.title: The Fund Returns
situations.question: Ganzouri wants the IMF loan back. Will you put your name behind it?
situations.body: Kamal Ganzouri reopens talks on the $3 billion stand-by loan cancelled in June. Net reserves have slid to about $18 billion. The Fund wants broad political backing. The Brotherhood refuses to endorse a debt it may inherit. Unions fear cuts to bread and fuel subsidies.

reasons.mb: We inherit no unpopular debt.
reasons.fel: Investors flee a state that refuses every rescue.
reasons.usa: Washington's offer spurned a second time.
reasons.army: No Fund inspectors near the military economy.

answers.sub: $3 billion on IMF terms: fuel subsidies trimmed, deficit capped.

reasons.fel: The pound steadies and the stock exchange breathes.
reasons.rev: The poor pay for the crisis while bankers smile.
reasons.mb: We will not inherit the Council's austerity.
reasons.army: Fund auditors will ask about state companies.

reasons.salc: The people's house, not Ganzouri, judges the debt.
reasons.fel: Months of waiting while the pound bleeds.

reasons.ksa: Riyadh dislikes handing the Brotherhood the purse.

situations.title: The Sukuk Bill

carrier.name: Osama Hamdy
carrier.role: clerk of the People's Assembly economic committee

situations.question: Nour wants Islamic bonds sold to the Gulf. Will you let the bill pass?
situations.body: Nour deputies table a bill for Islamic sukuk bonds backed by state assets. They promise Saudi and Qatari buyers by the billion. The Central Bank warns of pledging public land to foreigners. The tycoons call it amateur finance. Freedom and Justice fears being outflanked on faith.

reasons.ksa: Saudi banks gain a door into Egyptian assets.

reasons.fel: Clerics running the debt scares serious money.
reasons.rev: State land pawned to Gulf princes.

reasons.army: No foreigner holds a lien near military land.
reasons.salc: The people's Islamic choice traded for socialist bonds.
reasons.ksa: Riyadh's capital shut out of Egypt again.

reasons.mb: Islamic finance delayed again by the old bankers.
reasons.qat: Doha wanted an Islamic instrument for its money.

situations.title: Sixteen Billion

carrier.name: Farouk el-Okdah
carrier.role: Governor of the Central Bank of Egypt

situations.question: Reserves are near $16 billion. Will you pay the Brotherhood's price for the loan?
situations.body: Net reserves stand near $16 billion, about three months of imports. The Governor cannot defend the pound much longer; devaluation and import rationing loom. reasons.army: No Fund and no Brotherhood cabinet; the state holds.

reasons.rev: Prices jump overnight for every family.
reasons.salc: An interest-bearing loan signed without the people's deputies.

situations.title: The Red Line

carrier.name: Colonel Hesham Rifaat
carrier.role: liaison officer to the People's Assembly

situations.question: The defence committee wants the army's books. Will you open them?
situations.body: Freedom and Justice deputies on the defence and national security committee ask to review the military budget line by line. They also want the army's factories, hotels and land on the record. Sami Anan calls it the red line. American diplomats privately favour oversight.

reasons.army: Civilian scrutiny of our budget is the red line.

reasons.ksa: Riyadh wants an army answerable to no Islamist.

reasons.army: Our budget and businesses stay ours.
reasons.moi: A Council that keeps its secrets keeps ours.
reasons.mb: Elected deputies shut out of a vast economy.
reasons.usa: Congress keeps paying for books it cannot see.
reasons.rev: The generals' empire stays above the people.

situations.title: Promotion of Virtue

carrier.role: desk officer at the Interior Ministry

situations.question: Bearded men police the streets in God's name. Will you arrest them?
situations.body: Reports from Suez, Alexandria and Cairo describe bearded men harassing couples, unveiled women and shops selling music. answers.sub: Police round up the patrols; charges under the penal code.

reasons.ksa: The pious are trusted to correct the pious.
reasons.moi: Tolerated vigilantes make the police a joke.

reasons.usa: Rule of law for women and Copts.
reasons.salc: Enjoining good branded a crime by secularists.
reasons.moi: Civil prosecutors instead of our methods.
reasons.mb: Freedom talk today means attacks on religion tomorrow.

situations.title: The Gas Contract

carrier.role: legal adviser at the state gas company EGAS

situations.question: EGAS wants to cancel the Israel contract. Will you let it?
situations.body: The Sinai pipeline has been bombed more than a dozen times since February 2011. Gas to Israel has stopped for months, and EGAS says the buyer owes unpaid dues. answers.sub: Termination notice to the buyer; exports to Israel end.

reasons.mb: Parliament's demand met, and our deputies credited.

reasons.usa: Calm handling protects the peace Washington underwrites.
reasons.fel: No prosecutions if it stays commercial.
reasons.rev: The giveaway kept on Mubarak's terms.
reasons.mb: Parliament's will brushed aside by the generals.

situations.title: Abbasiya
situations.question: Your Defence Ministry is besieged. Will you send troops or let sheikhs mediate?
situations.body: Hazem Salah Abu Ismail's followers have camped outside the Defence Ministry in Abbasiya since his disqualification. Armed men in plain clothes attacked the sit-in at dawn; at least 11 are dead. Revolutionaries and Brotherhood youth march in support. Armour rings the ministry gates.

answers.sub: Troops clear Abbasiya; hundreds face military trials.

reasons.moi: Order restored, and our warnings vindicated.
reasons.salc: Our brothers before military courts again.

reasons.ksa: Riyadh admires a Council that does not bend.

answers.text: Negotiate through Salafist sheikhs for a peaceful withdrawal
answers.sub: Borhami's men talk the camp down; no military trials.

reasons.salc: We are the bridge between the state and its youth.
reasons.mb: No bloodbath the Islamist camp must answer for.
reasons.army: Generals bargaining with besiegers at their own gate.
reasons.moi: Sheikhs handed a role meant for the police.
reasons.rev: No new prisoners for the military courts.

answers.gripWhy: No troops and no trials; sheikhs mediate instead.

situations.title: Doha's Deposits

carrier.name: Amr Galal
carrier.role: aide at the Central Bank foreign desk

situations.question: Doha offers $2 billion in deposits. Will you take Qatari money?
situations.body: Qatar offers $2 billion in Central Bank deposits and investment pledges for the Suez Canal corridor. Doha's envoys speak openly of working with the next government, meaning the Brotherhood. Riyadh, which still owes much of its $4 billion pledge, warns against a Qatari foothold.

answers.sub: Reserves eased; Qatar becomes the Brotherhood's banker in Cairo.

reasons.qat: Doha's money buys a seat at Cairo's table.
reasons.mb: Our ally steadies the economy we will inherit.
reasons.ksa: A Qatari foothold in Cairo is Riyadh's red line.

answers.sub: Smaller Saudi-led Islamic financing; Doha snubbed, Salafist friends pleased.

reasons.salc: The Call's Gulf friends keep their place.
reasons.ksa: Saudi-led money keeps Cairo in Riyadh's orbit.
reasons.qat: Doha's offer thrown back in its face.
reasons.mb: Our ally's money refused for Saudi strings.
reasons.rev: One Gulf master swapped for another.

answers.text: Take neither; the army's own funds defend the pound
answers.sub: The military economy lends to the Central Bank; no Gulf strings.

reasons.army: The nation sees the army pay for its stability.
reasons.moi: Sovereign and strong, as the state should be.
reasons.qat: Doha's billions refused by the generals.
reasons.ksa: Riyadh's leverage shrinks along with Doha's.
reasons.mb: A drained treasury left for us to inherit.

callbacks.title: Arbitration over the Gas

carrier.name: Amr Galal
carrier.role: contracts officer at the state gas company

callbacks.question: Israel's buyers threaten arbitration. Will you keep the gas shut off?
callbacks.body: You halted gas exports to Israel after the pipeline bombing. East Mediterranean Gas now threatens international arbitration for billions. Washington's envoys mention the treaty. Delta factories, short of fuel, ask for the diverted gas.

answers.text: Send the gas to Egyptian factories at state prices
answers.sub: Export volumes go to the public sector and power plants.

reasons.rev: Egyptian gas fuels Egyptian workers, not Israeli plants.
reasons.army: Military factories get cheap gas too.
reasons.mb: Defying Israel's buyers plays well in every mosque.

reasons.mb: The Brotherhood cannot be seen softer on Israel.
reasons.usa: A religious embargo on Israel enrages Congress.
reasons.army: Holy-war talk near Sinai is a soldier's nightmare.
reasons.ksa: Riyadh wants no fiery adventures from Cairo.

callbacks.title: Principles or Rulings

carrier.name: Osama Nabil
carrier.role: clerk in the Council's legal office

callbacks.question: Will you let 'principles of Sharia' stand, or write 'rulings'?
callbacks.body: You adopted al-Azhar's Document as the constitution's basis. Now Salafist preachers demand Article 2 read 'the rulings of Sharia' and that al-Azhar's scholars vet every law. The Brotherhood wants 'principles' kept and parliament to decide. Coptic bishops warn of a theocracy.

answers.sub: The Document's wording holds; Islamist deputies will define Sharia.

reasons.qat: Doha's allies gain the power to interpret.
reasons.usa: The milder wording reassures Washington and the Copts.

answers.sub: Every law vetted for Sharia by senior scholars.

reasons.salc: Sharia's rulings bind the state, as the ancestors taught.
reasons.ksa: Riyadh welcomes a stricter Sharia clause.
reasons.mb: Clerics, not its deputies, will judge the laws.

reasons.usa: Washington hears theocracy in Egypt's constitution.

callbacks.title: Eid Meat from the Mosques
callbacks.question: Will you let Salafist mosques hand out the Eid meat and bread?
callbacks.body: In July you praised the Salafist Call's discipline in Tahrir. Now, before Eid al-Adha, its preachers ask to distribute subsidised bread and Gulf-funded sacrificial meat through their mosques in Alexandria and the Delta. The supply ministry's ration shops would stand aside.

answers.text: Let the mosques distribute; charity is a religious duty.

reasons.fel: Our clans lose their patronage to the sheikhs.

answers.text: Keep bread in the state ration shops, for all.
answers.sub: The supply ministry distributes Eid meat at subsidised prices nationwide.

reasons.army: The army's bakeries and the state keep feeding the people.
reasons.rev: Bread is a right, not a sheikh's favour.
reasons.mb: Better the state than the Salafists at the ration counter.
reasons.salc: The state shuts our charity to keep the poor dependent.
reasons.ksa: Riyadh's charity refused at its friends' door.

callbacks.question: Will you keep the Salafist committees at the polling stations?
callbacks.body: You let Salafist neighbourhood committees guard the polls in November. Judges in Alexandria and Kafr el-Sheikh now report men in the queues telling voters which list God wants. The Brotherhood files complaints. Runoffs open next week.

answers.text: Keep the committees; the pious keep better order.
answers.sub: Salafist volunteers stay at the stations through the runoffs.

reasons.usa: Observers report intimidation; the vote's credibility suffers.

answers.text: Send them home; let every party's agents watch.
answers.sub: Party delegates and judges alone supervise; the Brotherhood's agents everywhere.

reasons.mb: Our thousands of agents guard the ballot box properly.
reasons.usa: Party agents and judges look like a real election.
reasons.qat: A clean Islamist victory, certified by the ballot.
reasons.salc: Our volunteers dismissed so the Brotherhood can watch alone.
reasons.moi: Party agents at every station undercut police supervision.

callbacks.title: The First Sukuk Issue

carrier.name: Karim Abdel Aziz
carrier.role: bond desk officer at the Finance Ministry

callbacks.question: Gulf banks want Suez Canal revenue as collateral. Will you allow it?
callbacks.body: You backed Nour's sukuk bill, and the first issue is ready. Saudi and Qatari banks ask for Suez Canal revenue and state land as backing. Nasserist deputies recall the khedive's debts of 1875. Freedom and Justice wants its finance committee to name the Sharia board.

answers.text: Back the issue with taxes, never the canal
answers.sub: A smaller issue, no foreign lien on Suez or public land.

reasons.army: No foreign lien on sovereign ground.

reasons.ksa: Riyadh's banks refuse a weak guarantee.
reasons.qat: Doha's banks see thin returns.

answers.text: Pledge canal revenue; let the Sharia board approve
answers.sub: Full Gulf subscription; Salafist scholars sit on the board.

reasons.ksa: Saudi banks hold a claim on the canal.
reasons.army: A foreign lien on the canal touches sovereignty itself.

reasons.mb: Nour's scholars, not ours, hold the board.

answers.text: Let Freedom and Justice name the Sharia board
answers.sub: A Brotherhood committee controls issues; Qatari banks lead subscription.

reasons.mb: Islamic finance under the majority party's hand.
reasons.qat: Doha's banks lead the first issue.
reasons.salc: The Brotherhood steals the bill we wrote.
reasons.ksa: Doha's banks displace Riyadh's.
reasons.fel: Party committees running debt alarm the bankers.

carrier.name: Mahmoud Saeed
carrier.role: organiser of a Suez popular committee

callbacks.question: The patrols are spreading. Will you arm the neighbourhoods or trust the sheikhs?
callbacks.body: You left the virtue patrols to the sheikhs. Now they stop buses and close cafés in Suez and Ismailiya. A music shop has been burned. Popular committees from the January days offer to guard the streets. The Salafist Call says its own stewards will do it.

answers.text: Revive the popular committees under local councils
answers.sub: Workers and neighbourhood men patrol with council badges, not police.

reasons.moi: Civilian patrols usurp the police.
reasons.salc: Leftist gangs set against the pious.
reasons.army: Organised civilians are a risk to order.
reasons.fel: Committees of workers alarm business.

answers.gripWhy: Neighbourhoods police themselves without the security state.

answers.text: Let Salafist stewards keep the peace beside police
answers.sub: Salafist Call stewards patrol with police, under the sheikhs' word.

reasons.salc: The Call recognised as a guardian of the streets.
reasons.ksa: Pious order in Egypt's towns pleases Riyadh.
reasons.moi: Bearded deputies over our officers' heads.
reasons.rev: Morality militias, now with official blessing.
reasons.usa: Vigilantes with badges alarm Washington and the Copts.
reasons.mb: Nour wins the streets the Brotherhood wanted.

pending.line: Omar Suleiman has been without office since Mubarak's fall, yet the General Intelligence directorate he ran still holds the regime's files. Sami Anan urges the Field Marshal to sideline him and take the service under the Council. Riyadh and Washington prize him as their trusted channel to Cairo.

Central Bank Governor Farouk el-Okdah reports that Mubarak-era tycoons and foreign portfolio funds are draining dollars while the stock exchange stays shut. The Council must choose between capital controls with travel bans on businessmen, and open markets to reassure investors and the Gulf.

Mohamed Badie asks for a Brotherhood jurist on the committee drafting the constitutional amendments, which would amount to public recognition of the movement. The youth coalition and the liberal parties object to one movement holding a seat. The Salafist Call watches for any word on Article 2.

Crowds have broken into State Security Investigations headquarters at Nasr City and found files shredded and burnt. The new Interior Minister Mansour el-Essawy asks the Council to choose: dissolve the service and hand the surviving files to prosecutors, or rename it and keep its officers.

The revolutionaries, the Brotherhood and Washington demand a firm date for lifting the Emergency Law of the Mubarak years. The Interior Ministry insists it needs emergency powers while its police are still off the streets.

A mob has burnt the church at Sol in Atfih, and Copts are camped outside the Maspero building. Salafist sheikhs offer a customary reconciliation session. Pope Shenouda III's bishops and the revolutionaries demand prosecutions and a church rebuilt by the army.

Khairat al-Shater and other Brotherhood leaders are serving military-court sentences from the Mubarak years. Mohamed Badie asks for their release. The Interior Ministry warns of an emboldened Brotherhood, and Riyadh is alarmed.
The revolutionaries demand that leaders of the National Democratic Party be barred from the coming elections. Ahmed Shafik's allies and the provincial clans propose rebranding the party instead.

In Qena, Salafist preachers lead crowds blocking the railway against the new governor, a Copt and former police general. Essam Sharaf's cabinet asks the Council to stand by the appointment, freeze it, or send troops to reopen the line.

With its Freedom and Justice Party now founded, the Brotherhood asks for legal registration of the Society itself and its Muqattam headquarters. The Interior Ministry still keeps its old files on every member.

The Foreign Ministry floats restoring relations with Iran, and Egyptian intelligence prepares to host a Fatah-Hamas reconciliation. Riyadh and Washington frown. Nasserists, the Brotherhood and Doha cheer a foreign policy freed from Mubarak's alignments.

Military censors tell editors to clear every article about the armed forces in advance, and a blogger and a television host are summoned for insulting the army. The independent dailies, Al Jazeera and the US State Department protest.

Salafist crowds besieged churches in Imbaba over rumours of a convert held inside, and the night ended in deaths and a burnt church. Copts now demand the long-promised unified law on places of worship, and the Salafist Call rejects it. The Interior Ministry wants special powers in Giza.
Hamas and the Brotherhood press for the Rafah crossing into Gaza to open permanently. Washington and Israel warn against it, and the army fears for Sinai. Doha offers to fund the traffic.

Riyadh's $4 billion pledge must now take shape. Farouk el-Okdah wants Central Bank deposits to defend the pound, Riyadh prefers project grants released tranche by tranche at its discretion, and the generals want military-economy projects included.

Emad Abdel Ghafour's Nour Party applies for a licence, but the parties law bans parties founded on religion. The Brotherhood would rather not share the Islamist vote. Gulf-trained preachers promise a mass following.

Families of the martyrs camp in Tahrir. Mansour el-Essawy now proposes retiring hundreds of police generals and suspending officers charged with killing protesters. The ranks threaten to stay home and ask the Field Marshal to block the purge.

Essam Sharaf's cabinet drafts the first budget since the revolution. The unions demand a national minimum wage and permanent contracts for temporary workers. The business elite and Washington's economists warn of the deficit and falling reserves.

Abdel Fattah el-Sisi's Military Intelligence brings a dossier on foreign funding of April 6 and the rights groups, from American democracy institutes to Gulf donors. Publishing it and opening a judicial inquiry would brand the youth as agents and anger Washington.

Deputy Prime Minister Ali al-Selmi drafts supra-constitutional principles to bind the future constituent assembly. Sami Anan wants clauses keeping the military budget beyond parliament. The Brotherhood and the Salafists warn of the street.

Administrative courts annul Mubarak-era sales of public companies and state land. Workers demand renationalisation, while the tycoons and Gulf investors who bought the assets demand that the state appeal.

After crowds stormed the Israeli embassy, the Interior Ministry asks the Council to reactivate and widen the Emergency Law to cover strikes, road blocking and 'spreading rumours'. Revolutionaries and Washington see the promised lifting buried.

With the vote weeks away, revolutionaries and the Brotherhood demand the revived Treachery Law to bar former ruling-party officials. Old-party families in Upper Egypt threaten to block roads and railways if it is applied.

Twenty-eight Copts died at Maspero under army vehicles while state television urged citizens to defend the army, and the military prosecution has claimed the inquiry. Copts, revolutionaries and Washington demand a civilian investigation and accountability for the broadcast.

Riyadh slows its tranches while Gulf charities and preachers pour money into the Salafist Call's campaign. Restricting private Gulf funding of parties risks the Saudi deposits; tolerating it hands the Salafists an army of volunteers.

The al-Selmi document is now public. The Salafist Call and the Brotherhood call a mass Friday against it and demand the withdrawal of the clauses on military autonomy and on the constituent assembly. Sami Anan wants them kept, and the youth join the march.

As the Nour Party surges in the polls, its leaders call for segregated beaches and limits on alcohol for tourists. Hotel and tourism tycoons demand public reassurance from the Council. Salafist preachers warn the state not to defy the people's choice.

Security forces raided 17 democracy and rights groups, American institutes among them, and prosecutors now move to charge their staff. Washington demands the property back and hints at the aid. The Interior Ministry and Military Intelligence call it sovereignty.

For the uprising's first anniversary, the Field Marshal can lift the Emergency Law entirely, lift it except for 'thuggery', or keep it. Interior Minister Mohamed Ibrahim Youssef wants the exception kept; revolutionaries call it a loophole for everything.

The People's Assembly convenes under Speaker Saad al-Katatni with an Islamist majority. The Brotherhood demands the right to dismiss Kamal Ganzouri and form a government, and the Nour Party wants ministries too. The Council's declaration gives parliament no such power.

After 74 died at Port Said while police stood by, Ultras besiege the Interior Ministry. The People's Assembly demands Mohamed Ibrahim Youssef's dismissal and a full restructuring of the police. The ranks warn of a strike if officers are prosecuted.

Sixteen Americans are under a travel ban and US senators threaten the $1.3 billion in aid. Washington proposes bail and quiet departure. Nationalist papers and Brotherhood deputies demand the trial proceed, and the generals weigh the aid against their pride.

Generals and old-party men urge Omar Suleiman to stand for president as the state's candidate, though Sami Anan nurses ambitions of his own. Riyadh likes the former intelligence chief. Washington and the Brotherhood would see a restoration.

Deputies reject Kamal Ganzouri's programme, and the Brotherhood threatens to run its own presidential candidate unless it may form a government. The Council can keep Ganzouri, reshuffle with Brotherhood ministers, or call the bluff.

The Islamist majority fills the 100-member constituent assembly largely with its own. Liberals, al-Azhar and the Coptic Church walk out, and lawyers petition the courts. The Council can intervene, wait on the judges, or bless the assembly.

The Brotherhood nominates Khairat al-Shater for president, but his Mubarak-era military-court conviction may bar him unless the Field Marshal grants full rehabilitation. Doha favours him and Riyadh dreads him.

Parliament has passed a political isolation law aimed at Omar Suleiman and Ahmed Shafik. The Field Marshal must ratify it, refer it to the Supreme Constitutional Court, or sit on it as the candidate list closes.

Farouk Sultan's commission has disqualified ten candidates, among them Hazem Salah Abu Ismail, Khairat al-Shater and Omar Suleiman. Abu Ismail's followers besiege the commission. The Council must back its ruling or reopen appeals.

Protesters besiege the Saudi embassy over an Egyptian lawyer detained in the kingdom, and Riyadh recalls its ambassador with much of the pledge still undelivered. The Salafist Call and the business elite urge an apology; the revolutionaries demand the lawyer's release.

Ahmed Shafik and Mohamed Morsi head to the runoff. Old-party networks, police and state television line up behind Shafik, and the Brotherhood warns of fraud. The Field Marshal decides how neutral the state will appear.
Hamdeen Sabahi, third in the first round, demands a recount and the suspension of the runoff, and his Nasserist and youth supporters fill Tahrir. Both runoff camps court his voters.

Mamdouh Shahin drafts a supplementary constitutional declaration reserving military affairs to the Council, and legislative power too should parliament fall, after the handover. The Brotherhood and Washington would call it a soft coup.

Farouk Sultan's Supreme Constitutional Court hears the challenge to the election law, and Islamist deputies move a bill curbing the court. The Council must decide whether to defend the judges or bargain with a parliament it may soon lose.
